items.title: A signal that says nothing
items.prose: Over 200 trading days, a signal fired on 60 days. The stock rose on 33 of those and on 77 of the other 140 days.
items.question: Is the signal independent of up days?

options.text: Yes: the stock rose on 0.55 of days either way
No: the signal fired on only 60 days
options.why: How often the signal fires is not the test. Compare the share of up days with and without it.

options.text: No: 77 up days is far more than 33
options.why: You compared counts, not shares. 33 of 60 and 77 of 140 are both 0.55.

explain.text: $P(\text{up} \mid \text{signal}) = \tfrac{33}{60} = 0.55$ and $P(\text{up}) = \tfrac{110}{200} = 0.55$. The signal leaves the chance unchanged, so in this data it carries no information.

items.title: A clean year
items.prose: A fund loses money in a month with chance 0.3. Assume months are independent.
items.question: What is the chance of a year with no losing month? Give four significant figures.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Every month must avoid a loss: multiply twelve chances.

byKey.one: That is one month without a loss. All twelve must avoid one.
byKey.all: That is every month losing. The question asks for none losing.

explain.text: Each month avoids a loss with chance 0.7. Independence lets us multiply: $0.7^{12} = 0.01384$. Even a fund that wins 70% of months has a clean year only about once in 72.

items.title: Almost certain to win once
items.prose: A strategy wins each trade with chance 0.55, independently.
items.question: What is the smallest number of trades for which the chance of at least one win is 0.999 or more?

feedback.correct: $0.45^9 = 0.00076$ is the first power at or below 0.001.

byKey.add: You added 0.55 per trade until you passed 0.999. Chances of at least one do not add; use $1 - 0.45^n$.

items.title: Three assets, two coins
items.prose: Assets $X$ and $Y$ each rise or fall 1% with equal chance, independently. $Z$ falls exactly when $X$ and $Y$ move the same way.
items.question: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.why: Each pair is independent, but $X$ and $Y$ together fix $Z$.

options.text: All three rise together with chance $\tfrac{1}{8}$
options.why: If $X$ and $Y$ both rise, they moved the same way, so $Z$ falls. All three never rise together.

feedback.correct: Each pair is independent, yet $X$ and $Y$ together decide $Z$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the four equally likely states and check each statement.

explain.text: Given $X$ falls, $Z$ falls when $Y$ falls too: chance $\tfrac{1}{2}$. Given both fall, $Z$ falls for certain, so the three are not mutually independent. All three rising needs $X$ and $Y$ to rise, which forces $Z$ down: chance 0.

items.title: Two analysts agree
items.prose: The company beats earnings with chance 0.4. Each of two analysts says “beat” with chance 0.75 if it will beat and 0.25 if not. Given the truth, their calls are independent.
items.question: Both say beat. What is the chance the company beats?

widget.label: Chance of a beat given two beat calls

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use Bayes' rule with likelihoods $0.75^2$ and $0.25^2$.

byKey.one: That uses one analyst's call. Two independent-given-the-truth calls multiply their likelihoods.
byKey.lik: That is $P(\text{both say beat} \mid \text{beat})$. Bayes' rule turns it around.

explain.text: Given the truth, the calls are independent, so the likelihoods are $0.75^2$ and $0.25^2$. Bayes' rule gives $\tfrac{0.225}{0.225 + 0.0375} = \tfrac{6}{7} \approx 0.8571$. Analysts who copied each other would not be independent given the truth, and this would overstate the evidence.

items.title: A smaller book
items.prose: Five loans. A recession comes with chance 0.1 and sets each default chance to 0.32; otherwise it is 0.02. Given the regime, loans default independently. Each loan alone defaults with chance 0.05.
items.question: What is the chance that 2 or more of the five loans default? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find each regime's binomial tail, then weight and add.

byKey.indep: That is the binomial with $p = 0.05$, as if the loans were independent overall.
byKey.rec: That is the tail given a recession. Weight it by 0.1 and add the normal term.
byKey.recterm: That is the recession term alone. Add $0.9 \times 0.0038$ for normal years.
byKey.normterm: That is the normal-years term alone. Add the recession term, $0.1 \times 0.5125$.

explain.text: Given a recession, $P(K \ge 2) = 1 - 0.68^5 - 5 \times 0.32 \times 0.68^4 = 0.5125$. In normal years it is $1 - 0.98^5 - 5 \times 0.02 \times 0.98^4 = 0.0038$. So $P(K \ge 2) = 0.1 \times 0.5125 + 0.9 \times 0.0038 = 0.0547$.

items.title: Independence survives a complement
items.prose: Let $A$ and $B$ be independent. We show $A$ and $B^c$ are independent too.
items.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $P(A) = P(A \cap B) + P(A \cap B^c)$: $B$ and $B^c$ split $A$ into two disjoint parts
$= P(A)\,\big(1 - P(B)\big)$: take out the factor $P(A)$

feedback.correct: Split, rearrange, use independence, factorise, complement.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start by splitting $A$ along $B$.

explain.text: Splitting $A$ along $B$ isolates $P(A \cap B^c)$. Independence replaces $P(A \cap B)$ by a product, and factorising leaves $P(A)\,P(B^c)$. So news that $B$ did not happen is no news about $A$ either.

items.title: How much does a shared factor add?
items.prompt:
Two loans share an economy. A recession comes with chance $q$ and sets each default chance to $p_b$; otherwise it is $p_g$. Given the regime, the loans default independently. Let $D_1$ and $D_2$ be their default events.

(a) Find $P(D_1)$ and $P(D_1 \cap D_2)$.

(b) Show that $P(D_1 \cap D_2) - P(D_1)P(D_2) = q(1-q)(p_b - p_g)^2$.

(c) When are $D_1$ and $D_2$ independent? Can a shared regime make joint default less likely?

(d) Evaluate the difference for $q = 0.2$, $p_b = 0.2$, $p_g = 0.0125$, and say what it means for a lender.
items.model:
**(a)** By total probability over the two regimes, $$P(D_1) = q\,p_b + (1-q)\,p_g,$$ and the same for $D_2$. Call this $m$.

Given the regime, the loans default independently, so inside each regime the joint chance is a product. Then total probability gives $$P(D_1 \cap D_2) = q\,p_b^2 + (1-q)\,p_g^2.$$

**(b)** Expand the square: $$m^2 = q^2 p_b^2 + 2q(1-q)\,p_b p_g + (1-q)^2 p_g^2.$$

Subtract it from $P(D_1 \cap D_2)$, term by term. The $p_b^2$ terms give $q - q^2 = q(1-q)$. The $p_g^2$ terms give $(1-q) - (1-q)^2 = q(1-q)$. The cross term is $-2q(1-q)\,p_b p_g$. So $$P(D_1 \cap D_2) - P(D_1)P(D_2) = q(1-q)\big(p_b^2 - 2p_b p_g + p_g^2\big) = q(1-q)(p_b - p_g)^2.$$

**(c)** Every factor is at least 0, so the difference is never negative: a shared regime can only make joint default likelier. It is 0, and the defaults are independent, exactly when $q = 0$, $q = 1$ or $p_b = p_g$. Those are the cases with no real shared factor.

**(d)** With $q = 0.2$, $p_b = 0.2$, $p_g = 0.0125$: $m = 0.04 + 0.01 = 0.05$ and $P(D_1 \cap D_2) = 0.2 \times 0.04 + 0.8 \times 0.00015625 = 0.008125$. The formula gives $0.2 \times 0.8 \times 0.1875^2 = 0.005625$, which matches $0.008125 - 0.0025$.

So a double default is 3.25 times likelier than independence suggests. A lender who sizes capital for pairs of defaults with $0.05^2$ will hold too little against a recession.

rubric.text: Finds $P(D_1 \cap D_2) = q\,p_b^2 + (1-q)\,p_g^2$, using independence given the regime inside each branch.
Expands $P(D_1)P(D_2)$ and collects terms to reach $q(1-q)(p_b - p_g)^2$, with each step justified.
States the difference is never negative and is 0 exactly when $q \in \{0, 1\}$ or $p_b = p_g$.
Evaluates 0.005625, checks it against $0.008125 - 0.0025$, and explains the lender's understated joint risk.
